classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish genuinely different cube arrangements from rotations, then recognise that a three-cube bend in another plane is still an L-shaped prism. The second part requires extending the supplied same-level classification to unrestricted orientations.

children.label: a
children.prompt: On isometric paper, draw three cubes, all on the same level and stuck together to form a prism, in as many ways as you can. You will find that there are only two such prisms but different isometric drawings of each of them.

spec.description: Editable isometric dot paper supplied as requested drawing space.

answer.short: A straight row of three cubes and an L-shaped arrangement of three cubes. Rotations give other isometric drawings.
answer.worked: Keep the cubes joined face to face. Up to rotation, the three-cube arrangements are a straight row and an L. Each is an extrusion of its footprint through one cube height, so each is a prism.

spec.description: Representative straight and L tri-cube prisms.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Is it possible to make an object that is not a prism if the three cubes are stuck together such that each cube has at least one face stuck to the face of another cube?

answer.worked: Three face-connected cubes form either a straight row or an L, allowing rotations. Both have a uniform cross-section and are prisms.
